analysis.one_liner: Gives federal grants to states that create six-week paid parental leave programs run through private partners.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House bill to pay federal grants to states that create paid parental leave programs — backed by 9 cosponsors, 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans — has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no committee action since it was referred to six House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a grant program run by the Labor Department for states that have passed a paid family leave law. To get the money, a state's program must give new parents at least 6 weeks of partially paid leave for birth or adoption, with wages replaced at 50% to 67% depending on income. It would also build an interstate network to make state paid leave programs work the same way, and pay for it partly by cutting a $20 million federal enforcement fund to $10 million and terminating a named federal contract.
analysis.who_benefits: New parents in states that enact a paid leave law would get up to 6 weeks of partial pay, with the highest replacement rate (67%) going to workers near the poverty line. Small businesses would get grant help affording employer contributions. Private insurers and benefits administrators gain a required role: states must run the benefit through a "covered partnership" with at least one private entity, such as an insurance company. One national workforce organization would win a 5-year federal grant to run the interstate network's technology.
analysis.who_benefits_short: New parents, small businesses, private benefits administrators

how_it_helps.text: Creates a competitive Labor Department grant program, $1.5 million to $7 million per state, for states that have enacted a paid family leave program; the money can pay for startup costs, benefit payouts, software, outreach, and evaluation.

Sets a floor on what a qualifying state program must offer: 6 weeks of paid leave for the birth or adoption of a child, weekly benefits of 50% to 67% of the worker's earnings capped at 150% of the state's average weekly wage, with the 67% rate going to workers whose earnings are at or below the poverty line.
Directs the Labor Department to prioritize states with less paid-leave access today, plans that serve low-income populations, and financing that does not rely on federal money long-term.

Establishes the Interstate Paid Leave Action Network and $1.5-8 million 'conforming' and 'implementation' grants to harmonize state rules, process claims across state lines, and help small businesses afford employer payroll contributions.
The bill is bipartisan: it was introduced by a Republican with original cosponsors including Democrats, and has 9 cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund authorizations of roughly $39.8 million in 2026 rising to about $145.9 million in 2028, plus about $8.8 million a year for the network intermediary and $35.3 million a year each for two state grant pools. The bill pays for part of this by halving a $20 million federal enforcement fund to $10 million, ending a statutory funding stream for Defense Department golf courses, and terminating a named federal contract and rescinding its unspent balances. Workers and employers in participating states may also pay premiums or taxes under the state financing plans the bill requires them to establish.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, plus employers and workers in participating states

drawbacks.text: The benefit is narrow: it covers only birth and adoption, lasts at most 6 weeks, replaces only half of most workers' wages, and excludes anyone with less than 12 months on the job or fewer than 1,250 hours with that employer — leaving out many part-time, new, and high-turnover workers.

No one gets a federal guarantee. Only states that already passed their own paid leave law can apply, the grants ($1.5-8 million per state) are small relative to what these programs actually cost, and the bill prioritizes states that plan not to rely on federal funding — so whether any worker gets leave depends entirely on their state legislature.

States must deliver the benefit through a 'covered partnership' with a private entity such as an insurance company rather than through the state itself, and grant applicants get priority for using commercial off-the-shelf software — routing public money through private administrators and vendors.

The pay-fors are cuts elsewhere in government: halving a $20 million enforcement fund to $10 million, striking protections for Defense Department golf course funds, and terminating a specific named federal contract with its unspent balances rescinded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, honestly designed bill: it targets the right places (states with little paid-leave access and low-income workers, who get the richest benefit rate), demands self-sustaining state financing, and includes audits and public reporting. But its scale limits it — total authorizations of roughly $150-185 million a year across all states cannot fund a national program, the 6-week birth-and-adoption-only benefit is well short of what family and medical leave bills propose, and the FMLA-style eligibility test cuts out a large share of the low-wage workforce it is meant to help. The required private-sector partnership delivers the benefit but makes private insurers the permanent channel for it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them has held a hearing or taken any action on it since.

narrative.text: On April 30, 2025, Rep. Stephanie Bice introduced the bill with original cosponsors from both parties, including Democrats Houlahan, Stevens, and Gomez and Republicans Miller-Meeks, Letlow, and Feenstra.
The same day, it was referred to six House committees — Education and Workforce (first), Ways and Means, Armed Services, Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no vote, in any committee, since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet. The bill's potential beneficiaries — new parents in states that would adopt paid leave, and the private administrators who would run it — get nothing unless a committee moves it, while the status quo of no federal support for state paid leave programs continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits untouched in committee

for.name: Stephanie Bice
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 4 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Republican lead sponsor.

against.name: House committee chairs (Education and Workforce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Oversight, House Administration, Judiciary)
against.role: Chairs of the six committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Have taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since the bill was referred on April 30, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Support is bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with 9 cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans — and no vote has been taken, so there is no roll-call record to divide by party.

industries.note: The bill requires every qualifying state to deliver the benefit through a 'covered partnership' with at least one private entity, such as an insurance company, and must let employers self-administer — making private firms the permanent delivery channel wherever the grants drive state programs. Workers get the benefit and the administrators get the revenue, but public money flows through private hands to get there.
Grant priority goes to states using commercially available off-the-shelf software, and grant funds can buy and maintain that software — a guaranteed customer base for claims-processing vendors.

State paid leave programs can require employer contributions, but the bill lets small businesses get grant-funded help paying them, requires states to allow employer self-administration, and prioritizes reducing administrative burdens on employers.
One organization gets a 5-year federal grant (up to about $8.8 million a year) to run the interstate network's meetings, reporting, and technology.

analysis.trajectory: A bill referred to six committees and untouched since April 2025 is the classic profile of a bill that dies quietly: most measures with no committee action never reach a vote. Its bipartisan sponsorship could get it folded into a larger package if paid leave gains momentum, but on its own the lack of any hearing suggests neither committee leadership nor outside pressure has made it a priority this Congress.
